CycleAnalyzer · retrospective 2009-06-07 · model anchor 2009-05

DM+EM Cycle Monitor

Twenty-four economies read as mean-reverting cycles: where each one sits on the growth × inflation clock, what comes next and when, which cycles are not endangered, who stands apart from the global pack — and what all of it says to play in FX and yield curves.

Retrospective edition 2009-06-07. Information strictly before 00:00 Europe/Warsaw (2009-06-06T22:00:00Z). Monthly observations and their release vintages are separately dated below. Policy snapshots include only decisions already announced and effective. Negative FX funding costs are fully charged; a benign domestic cycle does not make a negative interest differential positive carry.

Reconstructed 2026-11-21 by applying the latest corrected methodology to historical inputs. The edition date identifies the information boundary; this is not a claim that these analyses or trades were published in 2009.

02Mean reversion & distance to danger

Each cycle variable is fit as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. The projected path (OU decay plus fading momentum) is tested against two thresholds: the inflation-fight line (+1σ) and the recession zone (−1σ). An economy whose path never gets near either is flagged not in danger — the cycle has far to run before it is endangered.

03The context filter — which extremes to fade, which to leave alone

Mean reversion alone is a bad idea. A z-score says a variable is far from equilibrium; it says nothing about whether the forces that created the extreme are done. Every stretch is cross-examined against the prevailing context — leading growth momentum, policy direction, real-rate restrictiveness, the clock heading — and against its own turn evidence:

EARLY TURN — the correction has begun but has retraced only a fraction of the extreme, and the context says the cycle change is coming anyway. The best entry: the top is already in, you ride the rest.
SETUP — still pinned at the extreme, but the leading indicators are deteriorating hard from the top. The counter-movement has not printed yet — position before it does.
TREND INTACT — stretched, but the context still feeds the deviation (an early hiking cycle behind a rich currency). Do not fade: the statistical pull earns zero weight until the context breaks.
LATE — the reversion has mostly happened; the edge is gone.

04What stands out vs the global cycle

Divergence is the signal: the first hiker in an easing world, the bank deliberating a hike while the pack is neutral, the one cutting into rising inflation. Each stance is scored against the universe median.

  • India — RBI runs a NEGATIVE real rate (-4.9%) with inflation +6.6pp above target — behind the curve.
  • Chile — BCCh runs a NEGATIVE real rate (-3.2%) with inflation +1.5pp above target — behind the curve.
  • United Kingdom — BoE runs a NEGATIVE real rate (-2.4%) with inflation +0.9pp above target — behind the curve.
  • Korea — BoK runs a NEGATIVE real rate (-1.6%) with inflation +0.6pp above target — behind the curve.
  • South Africa — SARB runs a NEGATIVE real rate (-1.5%) with inflation +4.5pp above target — behind the curve.
  • Hungary — MNB's real rate is +3.6pp above its own decade norm — most room in the universe to ease without stoking inflation.
  • Poland — NBP keeps cutting while inflation is above target and re-accelerating (+0.7pp over 3m) — credibility risk, watch the currency.
  • Norway — Norges Bank keeps cutting while inflation is above target and re-accelerating (+0.4pp over 3m) — credibility risk, watch the currency.
  • Mexico — Banxico runs a NEGATIVE real rate (-0.8%) with inflation +3.0pp above target — behind the curve.
  • China — PBoC's real rate is +2.5pp above its own decade norm — most room in the universe to ease without stoking inflation.

06FX scorecard

Each currency is scored against the USD as the sum of five engines — carry + cycle + valuation + momentum − penalty. The engines are deliberately built on different sources of return, so the sum is less about magnitude than about agreement: any single engine can be wrong for a year, but a currency where four pull the same way is wrong far less often. Components are scaled to comparable size (each contributes roughly ±0.5 to ±1.5): a total above ≈ +1 is a serious long candidate, anything below ≈ −0.5 is funding-leg material.

The five engines, one by one

Carry

0.25 × policy-rate differential vs USD, clipped ±6pp; positive pickup halved only when inflation gap eats it; negative funding costs fully charged

What it measures
The annualized interest differential you are paid — or pay — just for holding the currency versus USD, before anything moves. It is the only component that accrues to you every day the view is *wrong but not very wrong*.

Where the edge lies
Uncovered interest parity says forwards should price away the differential, so carry should net to zero. Empirically it does not — the forward premium puzzle: high-carry currencies depreciate less, on average, than their forwards imply, so rolling forwards harvests a persistent risk premium. That premium is compensation for crash risk: you collect it in calm regimes and give a slice back in risk-off. The model's refinement is that *nominal* carry which merely compensates for higher inflation is not edge at all — it is the currency's expected depreciation in disguise — hence the haircut when the inflation gap swallows the pickup, and the separate penalty beyond that.

Where it fails
in global vol spikes: carry is a crowded trade and unwinds violently, all pairs at once, regardless of local merit.

Cycle

phase value (Overheating +0.9, Goldilocks +0.6, Stagflation −0.6, Disinflation −0.9) × cycle amplitude (capped 1.5) × 0.5; when the clock's ETA to the next phase ≤ 9 months, half the weight shifts to the *destination* phase

What it measures
Where the economy sits on the clock, and — more importantly — where it is rotating to. Overheating and Goldilocks attract capital: rate expectations climb, equity and credit inflows follow. Stagflation and Disinflation repel it: cuts are coming, growth is going.

Where the edge lies
Markets are good at pricing the central bank's *last* move and bad at pricing the *rotation*. A currency entering Overheating will receive hikes that are not yet in the forwards; one rolling into Disinflation will receive cuts that are not either. The heading blend is deliberate: when rotation is fast you want to own the currency for what the cycle is about to do, not for where it stands. Amplitude scaling keeps direction honest — an economy hovering near the origin of the clock has a direction but no cycle, and direction without amplitude is noise.

Where it fails
when a supply shock masquerades as a cycle phase: oil-shock stagflation is bullish for an oil exporter's currency and bearish for an importer's, and the clock cannot tell them apart.

Valuation

−0.45 × REER deviation from its 10y average (z, clipped ±2.5), multiplied by the context-filter gate: ×1.25 on EARLY TURN, ×1.0 on SETUP, ×0.5 on WATCH, ×0.3 on LATE, ×0 on TREND INTACT

What it measures
How rich or cheap the currency is in *real, trade-weighted* terms — the BIS broad REER against its own decade. Real, so inflation differentials are already netted out; effective, so it measures competitiveness against all partners, not just the dollar.

Where the edge lies
Real exchange rates mean-revert over multi-year horizons through the competitiveness channel: a persistently rich currency erodes exports and the current account until the currency itself gives way, and vice versa. But the half-lives are long, which is exactly why this component is the one the context filter polices hardest: a cheap currency whose central bank is cutting into a slowdown is cheap *for a reason* and earns nothing (TREND INTACT ×0); the same cheapness with the correction already underway and the cycle turning earns a premium (EARLY TURN ×1.25). Valuation is edge only near turning points — the gate is what turns a slow anchor into a timing-aware signal.

Where it fails
when the fair value itself moves: a terms-of-trade regime shift (commodity supercycle, an energy transition) makes the 10-year mean stale, and the model will call 'rich' what is actually a new equilibrium.

Momentum

policy direction: hiking +0.4, on hold 0, cutting −0.4; +0.2 bonus for hiking while inflation momentum is already falling

What it measures
Which way the central bank is actually moving right now — not the level of rates (that is carry) but the direction of travel.

Where the edge lies
Policy cycles persist: hikes cluster, cuts cluster, and the first move is rarely the last, while FX over one-to-six-month horizons follows the *change* in rate differentials more than the level. The bonus case is deliberate and is the strongest single configuration in the stack: a bank hiking while inflation already falls is delivering rising *real* rates — the currency gets the differential and the credibility at once.

Where it fails
at the end of the cycle: the last hike is historically a sell signal, not a buy — the clock and the danger model are the overlays meant to catch the turn this component misses.

Penalty

−0.6 per pp of inflation gap beyond +2pp above target, capped at −3

What it measures
A credibility discount, not a return forecast. Beyond a couple of points above target, inflation stops being an input to carry and becomes the whole story: pass-through accelerates, expectations de-anchor, and the real value of the carry collapses faster than the nominal rate can compensate.

Where the edge lies
The edge here is *avoidance*: the cap at −3 encodes that past a point the right reading is 'uninvestable', not 'great short'. Shorting a 30–40% yielder pays ruinous negative carry, so a broken-credibility currency is excluded from the crosses on *both* sides — you neither hold it for the carry trap nor short it for the bleed. It re-enters the tradable universe only when disinflation is delivered, at which point the (still huge) carry starts counting again.

Where it fails
at the moment of a credible stabilization: the penalty lags the regime change, and the first year of a successful disinflation is historically the best carry trade there is.

How to read the sum

  • The edge is in the agreement structure, not the total. Carry confirmed by cycle and momentum — being paid to hold a currency whose central bank is hiking into an overheating economy — is the strongest configuration in the framework. Carry against cycle (a high yielder rolling into Disinflation, where the coming cuts will eat the differential) is the classic carry trap, and the sum catches it automatically: the cycle term goes negative before the carry term does.
  • A single-engine score is a watchlist item, not a trade. A total driven by valuation alone is precisely the 'mean reversion alone' mistake the context filter exists to block; a total driven by carry alone deserves a credibility check before anything else.
  • Why crosses instead of USD legs. The scores are measured vs USD, but the cleanest expression pairs the strongest long against the weakest credible funder: the dollar — with its own cycle, its own politics — nets out, leaving a relative-cycle position. Its actual policy-rate differential can be positive or negative; forward basis and trading costs also matter.
  • The penalty is a filter, not a signal. A deeply negative penalty (TRY-style) removes the currency from both sides of the book: the carry is uncollectible and the short bleeds. Uninvestable is a verdict too.
Worked example — TRY, this month's top score (+0.82): carry +1.50 from a +9.1pp policy-rate pickup over USD; cycle -0.56 from sitting in Stagflation and heading to Disinflation in ~0m; valuation +0.28; momentum -0.40 because TCMB is cutting. 2 engines pull for it, cycle and momentum against. The agreement structure, not any single number, is the trade.

The scorecard

Model crosses — strongest longs against the weakest credible funders (a broken-credibility high-carry currency is excluded from the short leg: shorting 30–40% carry is a bleed, not a hedge):

  • Long TRY / short CHF — edge +1.87. buy TRY, sell CHF via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +8.9pp annualized, before forward basis and costs
  • Long COP / short GBP — edge +1.63. buy COP, sell GBP via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +4.5pp annualized, before forward basis and costs
  • Long IDR / short JPY — edge +1.31. buy IDR, sell JPY via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +6.9pp annualized, before forward basis and costs

07What is most interesting to play

Each play states the exact legs to put on and the context check that licenses it — a stretch alone never does.

PLAY 1

Japan curve steepener

The Japan 10y−policy slope sits at +1.38pp (-0.4σ vs its own history, half-life 8m). The economy is in Disinflation, which pushes the slope steeper, and BoJ is cutting (-0.20pp over 6m at 0.10%) — with the long yield held fixed, that policy direction would tend to steepen the proxy, supporting the phase-led steepener call. The clock turns phase in ~5 months, so the window is now. Why not Poland, whose slope is more stretched (+1.8σ)? Because its stretch is TREND INTACT — NBP is still cutting, which keeps feeding the steepness — and a confirmed trend is precisely the extreme this framework refuses to fade on statistics alone.

How to express it
2s10s steepener in JPY: receive 2y swap (or long 2y govvies), pay 10y — DV01-neutral, so the P&L is the slope, not the level.

Context check
no meaningful stretch — this leg is not a mean-reversion bet.

Risk — A new growth or inflation shock can alter the phase, policy path and term premium. The measured slope is 10y minus policy, not an observed 2s10s spread; the 2s10s expression requires separate execution pricing and DV01 sizing.

PLAY 2

Long TRY / short CHF

The widest credible model-score gap is +1.87. Long TRY: carry +1.50, cycle -0.56 (Stagflation), valuation +0.28, momentum -0.40, credibility component +0.00. TCMB's calendar-based policy stance is cutting. Short CHF: carry +0.06, cycle -0.11 (Disinflation), valuation -0.60, momentum -0.40, credibility component +0.00. SNB's calendar-based policy stance is cutting. The indicative annual policy-rate differential is +8.88pp before forward basis and costs. A negative differential is a funding cost that the cycle/valuation view must overcome. The cross expresses a relative-currency view; the score is a heuristic, not a forecast return.

How to express it
buy TRY, sell CHF via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +8.9pp annualized, before forward basis and costs.

Context check
long leg REER: no meaningful stretch — this leg is not a mean-reversion bet. Short leg REER: stretch +1.1σ, already turning, 28% retraced; context score +0.58 → EARLY_TURN: the correction has started but only 28% of the extreme is unwound, and the surrounding cycle context points the same way — the rest of the move is the trade.

Risk — a global risk-off compresses EM carry crosses regardless of local cycles; the short leg rallies on safe-haven flows.

PLAY 3

The fresh signal: Poland

NBP keeps cutting while inflation is above target and re-accelerating (+0.7pp over 3m) — credibility risk, watch the currency. This is the 'one fresh signal' class of trade: the model singles out a policy divergence. A trade requires that this divergence is not already reflected in market prices; the monthly inputs do not measure forwards or the distribution of gains and losses.

How to express it
sell PLN vs a credible regional peer via forwards and put on a 2s10s steepener — easing into rising inflation ends with a weaker currency and a front-end repricing.

Context check
this is a divergence/momentum trade, not a fade: the fight line is not yet threatened, with inflation momentum +0.7pp over 3m — the context is moving *with* the position, which is what the filter requires when there is no extreme to revert.

Risk — single-meeting risk — one CPI print or one MPC vote can void the divergence; keep it tactical.

PLAY 4

The quiet carry: long MXN, because its cycle is not endangered

Mexico is the model's cleanest 'nothing breaks here' story: the OU projection keeps both the inflation gap and the growth cycle clear of danger thresholds for the whole 36-month horizon (phase: Stagflation). When the cycle is far from endangered the positive policy-rate differential offers indicative carry under a benign model path, while FX, duration and surprise risk remain — this is where 'we are ok with credit' applies: local-currency duration and credit both clip coupon while the clock stands still.

How to express it
long MXN vs USD via rolled 3m forwards (carry ≈ +5.1pp over USD), and/or unhedged local-currency 2–5y government bonds — the belly, not the long end, so the position is carry, not a duration view.

Context check
stretch +1.2σ, still pinned at the extreme; context score +0.83 → SETUP: the level itself has not budged, but the leading context is breaking against it hard — position for the counter-movement before it shows in the series.

Risk — the safety is model-projected, not guaranteed; a supply-side inflation shock (energy, food, FX pass-through) is exactly what an OU model cannot see coming.

PLAY 5

The reckoning trade: India front-end inflation repricing risk

A central bank holding a negative real rate (-4.9%) with inflation +6.6pp above target and momentum -0.8pp/3m eventually validates the market's fear, not its hope. The trade is in the front end, not the currency: INR is a second-order long *if* the bank moves, a short if it keeps refusing — so let rates carry the view.

How to express it
pay 2y INR swap (or short 2y govvies / front-end futures); keep duration elsewhere until the front end reprices the hikes.

Context check
this is a divergence/momentum trade, not a fade: already inside the inflation-fight zone, with inflation momentum -0.8pp over 3m — the context is moving *with* the position, which is what the filter requires when there is no extreme to revert.

Risk — the bank may be right — if growth cracks first, inflation dies on its own and paying the front end loses.

08Methodology

Clock
Growth z = OECD composite leading indicator's deviation from 100, scaled by 15y dispersion. Inflation z = CPI y/y minus the central-bank target, scaled likewise. Phase angle θ = atan2(infl, growth); rotation = median monthly Δθ over 9m.
Mean reversion
AR(1)/OU fit per series; expected path blends OU decay with fading 3-month momentum (the realistic rise-then-revert hump). Danger = the projected path crossing +1σ (inflation) or −1σ (growth); safe requires staying 0.6σ clear for 36 months.
Context filter
Every |z| ≥ 0.75 stretch is cross-examined: turn evidence (3m drift back toward the mean, share of the 12m peak already retraced) plus a context score from leading-growth momentum, real-rate restrictiveness, policy direction and the clock heading. Verdicts gate the mean-reversion terms in the trade models: TREND INTACT zeroes them, EARLY TURN boosts them.
Standouts
6m policy change vs universe median (robust MAD z), real-rate gap vs own decade, 3m inflation momentum → early hiker, deliberating hike, cutting into inflation, behind the curve, room to cut.
Data
Explicit historical input matrices only. The reviewed source ledger and country observation dates below govern this edition; the present-day repository cache is not an input.

Historical inputs and timing

Information cutoff: before 7 June 2009, 00:00 Europe/Warsaw (2009-06-06T22:00:00Z). Reconstructed on 2026-11-21. No archive of the present-day sources reaches back to 2009, so every input is either a real-time vintage, a decision history dated to the day, or a present-day history cut at an explicit, conservative publication gate; each one, with its availability bound, is in the ledger below. Projected paths are model scenarios, not realised outcomes.

Growth. 21 growth inputs are OECD composite leading indicators, amplitude adjusted, exactly as published in the May 2009 edition of the OECD real-time revisions database (Main Economic Indicators vintages, never revised afterwards; latest reference month 2009-03). That edition is used because its CLI was public by 2009-05-11 (dated public report quoting this edition's figures). Content check: the edition’s GBR aggregate for 2009-03 gives mom +0.30, yoy -5.42, matching the published mom +0.3, yoy -5.4. Evidence: Investment Executive, 'OECD indicator declines at slower rate in March', 11 May 2009: the CLIs for March continue to point to a strong slowdown, but France, Italy and the United Kingdom show tentative signs of, at least, a pause; the UK index increased by 0.3 point in March and was 5.4 points lower than a year ago (text as indexed by web search); Haver Analytics archive entry 'OECD LEIs The Long View', dated 11 May 2009; ECB Monthly Bulletin, May 2009: at its statistics cut-off of 6 May 2009 it cited the OECD CLIs for February, so the March-data release followed 6 May. Chile, Colombia and Thailand have no real-time leading indicator and no growth input; an input whose latest observation is more than 9 months older than the anchor month is not used (data notes below).

Inflation. Headline CPI y/y for 21 economies is computed inside a single real-time vintage: the OECD consumer-price index of the May 2009 edition, the newest edition whose month had ended before the cutoff (a conservative bound; no earlier publication date is claimed). China’s series is stored as an index of the same month of the previous year = 100, so its y/y is the value less 100. Australia and New Zealand publish quarterly CPI, repeated across each quarter’s three months. The United States uses the BLS CPI-U all-items NSA index from the ALFRED 2009-06-05 (Friday) vintage, latest 2009-04. Chile, Colombia and Thailand, and China (absent from the eligible real-time edition) use the present-day BIS CPI history requested only through 2009-04: a reference month is admitted once the whole following month has passed, although these offices publish within about ten days. Headline CPI y/y is rarely revised, but those histories are not vintages. Newer national releases that were public before the cutoff but are absent from the eligible vintage are not inserted, so an older observation date does not mean no newer release existed.

Exchange rates and yields. No vintage of the BIS broad real effective exchange rates for 2009 is retrievable. All 24 REER histories are present-day BIS broad indices requested only through 2009-04 (one full month after each reference month, against BIS publication around mid-month). Their later revisions — updated trade weights, revised consumer prices, a wider basket — are not removed; REER enters the model only through the valuation leg of the FX score. The 17 ten-year government yields are monthly market averages through 2009-05, the last completed month; market yields were observable as the month ended and are not revised.

Policy. Monthly policy histories are BIS end-of-month policy rates through 2009-05, the last completed month. The current effective snapshot is the rate in force on 2009-06-06 in the BIS daily decision history (downloaded only to that day): decisions announced but not yet effective at the cutoff are excluded. Policy rates are administrative facts, public when set, and are not revised. Changes are measured from the snapshot to exact completed-month anchors (3m: 2009-02, 6m: 2008-11, 12m: 2008-05). Policy instruments are those of the time (see the table); Mexico’s BIS series is the overnight interbank rate, a daily market rate until Banxico targeted it. Indicative carry is a policy-rate differential, not an executable forward quote; the curve input is the 10y yield minus the matched-month policy rate, not a traded 2s10s spread. OU horizons start at each series’ last eligible observation, so ETAs are not countdowns from the edition date.

Source observations missing inside the histories (no values are filled): policy/JP: 1999-03, 1999-04, 1999-05, 1999-06, 1999-07, 1999-08 … 70 more through 2006-02; y10/MX: 2001-08, 2001-09, 2001-11, 2007-10, 2008-02, 2008-05, 2008-09, 2009-01, 2009-04.

Inflation benchmarks are those publicly in force at the cutoff and are held constant through each historical fit. Four economies had no headline-CPI target: the Federal Reserve had no numerical target (2.0% is an analytical benchmark), the RBI's objectives referred to the wholesale price index, and the Bank of Thailand targeted core inflation; South Africa's targeted measure switches from CPIX to headline CPI with the January CPI. Benchmarks apply to the headline CPI series used here. Each benchmark is the target for the current calendar year as publicly known at the cutoff; China's is the government's annual CPI objective, announced each March (until then the previous year's applies). Where a range was set, its midpoint is used; for the euro area's ‘below but close to 2%’, 1.9%. Sources are listed only if published on or before the edition’s last eligible day.

Brazil4.50%CMN: 'Fixar para o ano de 2008 a meta para a inflação de 4,5%', tolerance ±2.0 percentage points. (IPCA, headline)CMN Resolution 3,378 of 29 Jun 2006; BCB Inflation Report, December 2007
Mexico3.00%'Annual CPI inflation of 3 percent' with a variability interval of ±1 percentage point. (INPC, headline)IMF Public Information Notice 07/140, Mexico Article IV, 13 Dec 2007; Banxico Inflation Report October–December 2007 and Monetary Program for 2008
South Africa4.50%'From January 2009, CPIX inflation will be replaced by a new inflation target measure, headline CPI'; 'the target band for headline CPI will remain unchanged at 3-6 per cent' (midpoint 4.5%). (headline CPI (CPIX until the December 2008 data))National Treasury, 2008 Medium Term Budget Policy Statement, ch. 2, 21 Oct 2008
Turkiye7.50%End-year CPI inflation target for 2009 of 7.5% (uncertainty band ±2 percentage points), proposed by the CBRT on 3 Jun 2008 and accepted by the Government; targets are set jointly as point targets for a three-year horizon. (CPI, headline, end-year)CBRT No. 2008-14, Open Letter to the Government about inflation targets, 3 Jun 2008; CBRT, Monetary and Exchange Rate Policy for 2009, 16 Dec 2008
Poland2.50%Continuous CPI target of 2.5% with a ±1 percentage-point tolerance band. (CPI, headline)NBP Inflation Report, October 2007; NBP Inflation Report, February 2008
Hungary3.00%'An inflation rate near the 3 per cent medium term objective.' (CPI, headline)MNB Quarterly Report on Inflation, November 2007; MNB Quarterly Report on Inflation, February 2008
Czechia3.00%'The current target of the Czech National Bank (CNB) of 3%' (in effect since January 2006), tolerance ±1 percentage point. (CPI, headline)CNB press release, 8 Mar 2007
Indonesia4.50%Government inflation target for 2009 of 4.5% ±1% (Finance Minister decree No. 1 of January 2008, setting the target path); not formally revised, although Bank Indonesia's projections for the year were higher. (CPI (IHK), headline)Bank Indonesia, Laporan Perekonomian Indonesia 2007 (box: Sasaran Inflasi)
Korea3.00%Medium-term target of 3.0% ±0.5% on headline CPI inflation for the three years starting 2007, judged on the three-year average (resolution of 17 Aug 2006). (CPI, headline)Bank of Korea press release, medium-term inflation target, 17 Aug 2006 (redistributed on Newswire); IMF Country Report 07/344, Korea Article IV, October 2007; IMF Public Information Notice 08/117, Korea Article IV: 'the Bank of Korea's target of 2½–3½ percent'
Chile3.00%'Keep annual CPI inflation around 3% most of the time, within a tolerance range of plus or minus one percentage point.' (CPI, headline)Central Bank of Chile, Monetary Policy in an Inflation Targeting Framework, January 2007
Colombia5.00%'Fijó la meta de inflación para el año 2009 en el rango entre 4.5% y 5.5%, con 5% como meta puntual para efectos legales' (Board decision of 21 Nov 2008). (CPI, headline, December y/y)Banco de la República, Board communiqué, 21 Nov 2008; Banco de la República, 'Inflation target set at 5% for 2009'
Thailand1.75%Core inflation target 0–3.5% (quarterly average) remains in force; the MPC and the Minister of Finance have proposed a range of 0.5–3.0% for the year, awaiting Cabinet approval (midpoint 1.75% either way). (Core CPI; benchmark applied to headline CPI)BoT Inflation Report, October 2008; BoT Inflation Report, January 2009 (box: Setting an appropriate inflation target)

Japan: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA JPN); United Kingdom: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA GBR); Brazil: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA BRA); Mexico: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA MEX); South Africa: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA ZAF); Turkiye: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA TUR); Poland: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA POL); Hungary: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA HUN); Czechia: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA CZE); Indonesia: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA IDN); Korea: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the May 2009 edition (real-time database, LI_AA KOR); Chile, Colombia, Thailand: no real-time growth input.

Data notes: cpi/CN: absent from the May 2009 CPI edition; the present-day BIS history behind the one-full-month publication gate (latest 2009-04) is fresher than any of the previous 3 editions and is used. policy/IN: BIS monthly differs from the daily month-end in 2007-03; monthly rows retained.
